summary: Updates the 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery protocol of RFCs 6775 and 8505 with Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery, which protects the owner of an address against theft and impersonation in low-power and lossy networks. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: AP-ND helps a low-power IPv6 device prove that it owns an address before a router accepts or changes its registration. The device uses a public-key-derived identifier and signs a challenge, making it harder for another node to claim that address.

subtitle: How a low-power IPv6 node proves ownership of an address during neighbor discovery.

tldr.problem: A 6LoWPAN node can impersonate another registered address if it can spoof the ownership value derived from a link-layer address.
tldr.mechanism: Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery uses a Crypto-ID derived from a public key, then challenges the registering node to sign a message containing the address and fresh nonces.
tldr.outcome: After ownership is validated, only the owner can change the registration, supporting source-address validation. RFC 8928 updates RFC 8505 and is updated by RFC 9926 and RFC 9927.

facts.label: Recommended Crypto-ID length
facts.value: 128 bits; at least 64 bits for compatibility

today: RFC 8928 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 8505. It has been updated by RFC 9926 and RFC 9927.

sections.title: Address Theft in 6LoWPAN
sections.content:
6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery lets a node register an IPv6 address with a nearby 6LoWPAN Router (6LR), which relays registrations to a 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR). RFC 8505 adds a Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR) to associate an address with its owner.

A ROVR can be derived from an EUI-64 link-layer address, but that address can be spoofed. A node that learns the registered address and ROVR could then imitate the owner, take over the registration and redirect traffic.

Address-Protected Neighbor Discovery (AP-ND) uses a cryptographic identifier, or Crypto-ID, in the ROVR field and requires proof of ownership before a 6LR creates or changes registration state.
sections.plainLanguage: A device could steal an IPv6 address if it can copy the value used to identify that address's owner. AP-ND adds a cryptographic proof before a router accepts registration changes.

sections.title: The Crypto-ID
sections.content:
The Crypto-ID is derived from a public key and other parameters, then carried in the ROVR field of an EARO. Its use is the recommended way to compute a ROVR. The EARO's new C flag indicates that the ROVR is a Crypto-ID and that the node may be challenged.

A hash function associated with the chosen signature scheme is applied to the Crypto-ID Parameters Option (CIPO), with reserved and padding bits set to zero. The leftmost bits of the resulting hash form the identifier. A 128-bit Crypto-ID is recommended; at least 64 bits are needed for backward compatibility with RFC 8505.

The CIPO carries the public key and parameters, the NDP Signature Option (NDPSO) carries the signature, and a Nonce Option carries challenge data. The registered IPv6 address is not derived from the key.
sections.plainLanguage: The Crypto-ID is made from a public key and parameters and is stored with the registered address. Later, the device proves it owns the matching private key by signing a challenge.

sections.title: EARO, CIPO and NDPSO Fields
sections.content:
The Enhanced Address Registration Option (EARO), option type 33, gains a C flag. When set, the ROVR field contains a Crypto-ID. The extension reuses the RFC 8505 status codes Validation Requested and Validation Failed.

The Crypto-ID Parameters Option (CIPO), option type 39, carries a public key, a Crypto-Type, a modifier and the associated EARO length, with padding to an eight-octet boundary. A modifier allows one key pair to produce multiple Crypto-IDs.

The NDP Signature Option (NDPSO), option type 40, carries a signature. The receiver finds the matching CIPO using the leftmost 128 bits of the EARO's ROVR. A message containing an NDPSO must contain exactly one EARO whose Crypto-ID is associated with the signing key. The 6CIO also gains an A flag to indicate that AP-ND is activated in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration option identifies the Crypto-ID, the CIPO carries the public key and parameters, and the NDPSO carries the proof. A capability flag tells nodes when AP-ND is active across the network.

sections.title: Challenge and Ownership Proof
sections.content:
A node first sends a Neighbor Solicitation with an EARO whose C flag is set. If the 6LR has no consistent state for the node, it replies with a Neighbor Advertisement marked Validation Requested and includes a nonce.

The node retries with an NS containing the EARO, CIPO, its own nonce and the NDPSO signature. Both nonces are included in the signed material. The 6LR recomputes the Crypto-ID, checks that it matches the ROVR and verifies the signature.

On success, the 6LR forwards the registration to the 6LBR using EDAR and EDAC. On failure, it returns Validation Failed. When AP-ND is active, the 6LR must challenge before creating a Crypto-ID binding or changing a validated binding's parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The router sends a fresh challenge, and the device signs the challenge together with its address and its own nonce. The router accepts the registration only if the signature proves the device holds the matching private key.

sections.title: Supported Signature Schemes
sections.content:
AP-ND defines three Crypto-Types. Type 0 is ECDSA with the NIST P-256 curve and SHA-256 and must be supported by all implementations. Type 1 is Ed25519 with SHA-512 and may be supported. Type 2 is ECDSA over Wei25519 with SHA-256 and may also be supported.

The signed data includes a 128-bit message-type tag, the CIPO, the 16-byte target address, the nonce from the 6LR, the nonce from the node and the one-byte EARO length. The signature size for each of the three types is 64 bytes.

The 6LR must validate the public key and regenerate the Crypto-ID from the CIPO before verifying the signature. Implementations must not reuse a private key across signature schemes or for purposes other than NDPSO signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: All implementations must support ECDSA256; two other schemes are optional. The signature covers the address, key parameters and both nonces, so the proof is tied to this registration challenge.

sections.title: Security Limits and Deployment
sections.content:
Protection is effective only when the 6LRs in the network support AP-ND. In a mixed network, an attacker may register through a legacy router even if the network's activation flag is set.

The 6LBR trusts the 6LR to verify the proof, so communication between them must be protected. A compromised 6LR that knows an owner's ROVR could claim the owner has moved and redirect traffic. A rogue node can also consume registration state; a 6LR must reject excess registrations with Neighbor Cache Full.

Nonces should not repeat. A Crypto-ID of at least 64 bits has a 0.01% collision probability for a network of 66 million nodes, according to the RFC. Nodes are recommended not to derive the IPv6 address from the ROVR.
sections.plainLanguage: All relevant routers need to enforce the challenge or a legacy router can leave the network exposed. The 6LR must protect its registration resources, and the 6LBR must trust its 6LR to verify each proof correctly.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA created a Crypto-Types subregistry for the signature schemes used by AP-ND. The initial entries are type 0 ECDSA256, type 1 Ed25519 and type 2 ECDSA25519.

IANA assigned IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option type 39 to the CIPO and type 40 to the NDPSO. It also assigned 6LoWPAN Capability Bit 9 to AP-ND Enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA lists the signature types, the two new Neighbor Discovery options and the capability bit that indicates AP-ND support. These shared assignments let different implementations interpret the fields consistently.
